solution.concept_anchor: BLRC under T.K. Viswanathan and IBC genesis
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because the Nachiket Mor Committee is a well-known RBI committee on financial inclusion, making it a plausible but entirely wrong attribution for the insolvency reform body.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Nachiket Mor Committee was constituted by RBI for financial inclusion — unrelated to insolvency law reform.
Eliminate (c): The Raghuram Rajan Committee was an expert group on financial sector reforms, not specifically on bankruptcy law.
Eliminate (d): The N.L. Mitra Committee was related to legal framework for the financial sector but predates and is distinct from the BLRC.
Confirm (b): The Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee was chaired by T.K. Viswanathan, a former Law Secretary, and its 2015 report formed the blueprint for IBC 2016.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students familiar with financial sector committees often confuse the BLRC with other reform panels. The Nachiket Mor Committee and Rajan Committee are prominent names in economy, making them attractive distractors. A student who has only surface knowledge may associate 'bankruptcy reform' with any high-profile financial expert, rather than specifically recalling T.K. Viswanathan — a less headline-grabbing but precisely correct answer.
solution.final_explanation:
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 emerged from a comprehensive reform process triggered by the failure of earlier fragmented frameworks like SICA, SARFAESI, and RDDBFI to resolve stressed assets efficiently. The Government of India constituted the Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee (BLRC) to design a consolidated insolvency framework.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Nachiket Mor Committee (2013) was an RBI committee on comprehensive financial services for small businesses and low-income households — unrelated to insolvency.
• Option (b) — Correct: The BLRC was chaired by T.K. Viswanathan, former Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha and Law Secretary. Its 2015 report recommended consolidating 12+ laws into a single code.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Raghuram Rajan chaired an expert group on making Mumbai an international financial centre (2007), not the insolvency reform body.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: N.L. Mitra chaired an earlier committee on legal aspects of the financial sector but is not associated with IBC's immediate drafting.

Value Addition:
• IBC 2016 consolidated and repealed laws including SICA 1985 and amended SARFAESI, Companies Act, and RDDBFI Act.
• The BLRC recommended a time-bound, creditor-friendly process — a philosophical departure from debtor-friendly SICA.
• Constitutional backing for IBC comes from Entry 9 (Insolvency) of the Concurrent List — Parliament can legislate, and does so with overriding effect.

solution.concept_anchor: IBBI composition and dual regulatory character

statement_analysis.statement: IBBI is a constitutional body established under Article 239 of the Constitution of India.
statement_analysis.reason: IBBI is a statutory body established under Section 188 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 — it derives its existence from legislation, not the Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: IBBI performs both a regulatory function over insolvency professionals and an oversight function over the insolvency resolution processes — a combination unique among Indian financial regulators.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike SEBI or RBI which regulate markets/banks but not the resolution processes themselves, IBBI uniquely combines regulation of professionals (IPs, IPAs, IUs) with oversight of CIRP and liquidation processes.

statement_analysis.statement: The ex-officio members of IBBI include nominees from the Reserve Bank of India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 188 of IBC specifies that IBBI has three ex-officio members who are nominees of RBI, SEBI, and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, alongside the Chairperson and five whole-time members.

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student who incorrectly believes IBBI is a constitutional body (confusing it with bodies under Part XIV of the Constitution) will eliminate statement 1 as correct and then doubt whether 2 and 3 alone can constitute the answer, being drawn toward 'd' if they also misread statement 3.
elimination_logic: Eliminate any option that includes Statement 1 as correct — IBBI is a statutory body under Section 188 of IBC, not a constitutional body.
Confirm Statement 2 as correct — IBBI's dual character as both regulator and process-oversight body is its defining institutional feature.
Confirm Statement 3 as correct — RBI, SEBI, and MCA nominees serve as ex-officio members, a provision explicitly in Section 188.
The combination 2 and 3 only points to option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'constitutional vs. statutory' trap is a perennial UPSC favourite. Students aware that IBBI was 'created by Parliament' sometimes incorrectly extend this to 'constitutional body,' conflating legislative creation with constitutional status. Additionally, the specific composition — three ex-officio members from RBI, SEBI, and MCA — is a detail that can be confused with the composition of other multi-regulator bodies like the Financial Stability and Development Council.
solution.final_explanation:
IBBI was established under Section 188 of the IBC, 2016 — it is a statutory body accountable to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. It is not a constitutional body, unlike the CAG or Election Commission.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: IBBI has no constitutional basis; it was created by an Act of Parliament. Article 239 relates to administration of Union Territories — entirely unrelated.
• Statement 2 — Correct: IBBI's dual role — regulating professionals (IPs, IPAs, IUs) AND overseeing resolution processes (CIRP, liquidation) — makes it institutionally unique. RBI regulates banks but does not oversee the resolution process; SEBI regulates markets but not resolution professionals.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The ex-officio members are nominees of RBI, SEBI, and MCA — providing inter-regulatory coordination. The full board comprises one Chairperson, five whole-time members, and these three ex-officio members.

Value Addition:
• IBBI headquarters is in New Delhi; it reports to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
• The Chairperson and whole-time members are appointed by the Central Government.
• IBBI's quasi-judicial function is exercised through an Adjudicating Officer mechanism — maintaining separation between regulatory and disciplinary functions.

solution.concept_anchor: IBBI regulatory jurisdiction over IPs, IPAs, IUs — not NCLT

statement_analysis.statement: IBBI directly regulates Adjudicating Authorities such as the National Company Law Tribunal and the Debt Recovery Tribunal.
statement_analysis.reason: IBBI has NO regulatory jurisdiction over NCLT or DRT — these are judicial/quasi-judicial bodies under the Ministry of Law. IBBI regulates only IPs, IPAs, IUs, and IPEs.

statement_analysis.statement: Insolvency Professional Entities (IPEs) are a category of regulated entities distinct from both Insolvency Professionals and Insolvency Professional Agencies.
statement_analysis.reason: IPEs were added as a separate regulated category — they are firms through which IPs operate, distinct from individual IPs and from IPAs which are self-regulatory enrollment bodies.

statement_analysis.statement: Among the processes over which IBBI has jurisdiction is the Pre-packaged Insolvency Resolution Process, in addition to CIRP and liquidation.
statement_analysis.reason: IBBI's jurisdiction covers CIRP, Liquidation, PPIRP (introduced via 2021 amendment for MSMEs), and personal insolvency — all insolvency-related processes under IBC.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that IBBI oversees the insolvency ecosystem may loosely associate it with 'overseeing' NCLT proceedings and thus mark Statement 1 as correct, not recognising that regulatory oversight of a process differs fundamentally from jurisdiction over an adjudicating authority.
elimination_logic: Identify Statement 1 as the clearly incorrect one — IBBI has no power over NCLT or DRT, which are judicial bodies outside IBBI's regulatory perimeter.
Confirm Statement 2 as correct — IPEs are a distinct fourth category of regulated entities introduced after the original three (IPs, IPAs, IUs).
Confirm Statement 3 as correct — PPIRP falls squarely within IBBI's regulatory oversight as a process under IBC.

The option identifying only Statement 1 as incorrect is option (a) — but since the stem asks which is NOT correct, the answer is (a)... Re-check: '1 only' as the incorrect statement maps to option (a) per the stem 'which is NOT correct' → correct_option is 'a'. Wait — re-reading: options are (a)1 only (b)2 only (c)both (d)neither. Statement 1 is the only incorrect one → answer is (a). Correction applied: correct_option should be 'a'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The confusion between IBBI's oversight of insolvency processes and jurisdiction over adjudicating authorities is a structurally common trap. Students who know that IBBI 'oversees' the insolvency system may incorrectly infer it also 'regulates' the tribunals. In reality, NCLT and DRT are part of the judicial hierarchy — their functioning is governed by the Ministry of Law, not IBBI.
solution.final_explanation:
IBBI's regulatory perimeter is precisely defined under IBC. It covers Insolvency Professionals (IPs), Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPAs), Information Utilities (IUs), and subsequently added Insolvency Professional Entities (IPEs). What IBBI does NOT regulate are the adjudicating authorities — NCLT and DRT — which are judicial/quasi-judicial bodies.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: IBBI cannot issue directions to NCLT or DRT. These tribunals derive their powers from the Companies Act and RDDBFI Act respectively and report through the judicial hierarchy.
• Statement 2 — Correct: IPEs are firms (partnerships or companies) of insolvency professionals through whom IPs can operate. They are distinct from IPs (individuals) and IPAs (enrollment/regulatory SROs).
• Statement 3 — Correct: IBBI's process jurisdiction includes CIRP, liquidation, PPIRP (2021 for MSMEs), and the personal insolvency processes under Part III of IBC.

Value Addition:
• The four regulated entity categories under IBBI: IPs, IPAs, IUs, and IPEs — a common enumeration question.
• NCLT appeals go to NCLAT and then Supreme Court — IBBI has no appellate role.
• IBBI also issues regulations under Section 196 of IBC — it has broad delegated legislative power.

solution.concept_anchor: CIRP initiation — sections, creditor types, threshold

statement_analysis.statement: A Financial Creditor may initiate CIRP by filing an application under Section 7 of IBC.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 7 explicitly provides the right of a Financial Creditor to initiate CIRP upon proof of default — no prior notice to the corporate debtor is required.

statement_analysis.statement: An Operational Creditor must issue a 10-day demand notice to the Corporate Debtor before filing an application for initiation of CIRP under Section 9.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 8 of IBC requires an Operational Creditor to deliver a demand notice; only after 10 days without payment or dispute can they file under Section 9.

statement_analysis.statement: The minimum default threshold for initiating CIRP against a company, as originally enacted in IBC 2016, was ₹1 crore.
statement_analysis.reason: The original threshold under Section 4 of IBC 2016 was ₹1 lakh — it was raised to ₹1 crore during the COVID-19 pandemic via the IBC (Amendment) Ordinance 2020 to prevent pandemic-related CIRP filings.

statement_analysis.statement: Homebuyers in a real estate project were classified as Financial Creditors through a 2018 amendment to IBC, upheld in the Chitra Sharma case.
statement_analysis.reason: The IBC (Second Amendment) Act 2018 inserted a proviso to Section 5(8)(f) classifying allottees of real estate projects as Financial Creditors — this was challenged and upheld by the Supreme Court in Pioneer Urban Land vs. Union of India (related to the Chitra Sharma litigation).

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student who knows the ₹1 crore figure as the 'current' threshold but does not recall it was a COVID-era amendment (not the original) will mark Statement 3 as correct, pushing the count to 'all four' and selecting (d).
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 as correct — Section 7 gives Financial Creditors the right to directly file before NCLT on proof of default.
Confirm Statement 2 as correct — the 10-day demand notice under Section 8 is a mandatory precondition for Operational Creditors.
Eliminate Statement 3 as correct — the original threshold was ₹1 lakh; ₹1 crore was set only by the 2020 COVID ordinance.
Confirm Statement 4 as correct — homebuyers as Financial Creditors was a 2018 amendment, judicially affirmed in the Chitra Sharma/Pioneer Urban case.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap here is the ₹1 crore threshold. Because ₹1 crore is the current operative threshold and is the figure most candidates have memorised, they often forget it was ₹1 lakh originally. The question tests whether the student understands that the threshold was amended — a fact that changes the verdict on Statement 3 from 'correct' to 'incorrect,' shifting the total count from four to three.
solution.final_explanation:
CIRP can be triggered by three categories of applicants under different sections of IBC, each with distinct procedural requirements.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 1. Financial Creditor — Section 7 | Correct |
| 2. Operational Creditor — 10-day notice then Section 9 | Correct |
| 3. Original threshold was ₹1 crore | Incorrect |
| 4. Homebuyers as Financial Creditors — 2018 amendment | Correct |

Statement 3 is the trap — the original Section 4 threshold was ₹1 lakh. The ₹1 crore figure came from the IBC (Amendment) Ordinance, March 2020, issued to prevent pandemic-triggered insolvency filings from overwhelming the system. Three statements are correct → option (c).

Value Addition:
• The Corporate Debtor itself can initiate CIRP under Section 10 — a rarely tested but examinable provision.
• A Financial Creditor files jointly with related party creditors excluded; an Operational Creditor must show a genuine dispute does not exist.
• The Chitra Sharma case was the original writ petition; the landmark judgment classifying homebuyers as Financial Creditors is Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure vs. Union of India (2019).

Key Supreme Court Judgments Shaping IBC Jurisprudence

solution.concept_anchor: IBC Supreme Court judgments and their core holdings
solution.strong_distractor: b — The Essar Steel judgment involved both Section 29A and CoC powers, making students likely to attribute the 'CoC commercial wisdom' doctrine to the Arcelormittal case instead, which also involved Section 29A but on eligibility grounds.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Swiss Ribbons (2019) — this is the case that tested IBC's constitutional validity and the Financial vs. Operational creditor distinction; maps to item A → 2.
Anchor on Essar Steel (2019) — CoC's commercial wisdom as supreme and the binding nature of approved plans; maps to B → 4.
Arcelormittal vs. Satish Kumar Gupta dealt with Section 29A's strict interpretation on connected persons for resolution applicant eligibility; maps to C → 1.
Vidarbha Industries (2022) introduced judicial discretion for NCLT in admitting Section 7 applications; maps to D → 3.
This gives A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Essar Steel and Arcelormittal cases both arose from the same stressed asset ecosystem and involved overlapping issues of Section 29A and creditor treatment. Students frequently conflate the two. Essar Steel's primary ratio is CoC commercial wisdom and equal-but-not-identical treatment of creditors; Arcelormittal's primary ratio is the strict interpretation of 'connected persons' under Section 29A for resolution applicant eligibility.
solution.final_explanation:
Four landmark Supreme Court judgments have shaped IBC jurisprudence fundamentally.

List I (Case) matches with List II (Core Holding):
• A → 2: Swiss Ribbons (2019) upheld IBC's constitutional validity and justified differential treatment of Financial and Operational Creditors on grounds of rational classification.
• B → 4: In the Essar Steel case (2019), the Supreme Court affirmed that the Committee of Creditors' commercial wisdom is paramount — courts cannot second-guess the economic merits of a resolution plan.
• C → 1: Arcelormittal vs. Satish Kumar Gupta involved a strict reading of Section 29A — specifically the 'connected persons' disqualification that extends the promoter bar to related entities.
• D → 3: The Vidarbha Industries judgment (2022) controversially held that NCLT has discretion to admit or reject a Section 7 application even when default is established — not an automatic admission.

The trap pairing is B and C — both arose from large steel sector insolvencies and involve overlapping themes but distinct ratios.

Value Addition:
• Swiss Ribbons is the foundational IBC constitutionality case — always cite it when IBC's legal validity is questioned.
• Ghanashyam Mishra (2021) SC held that government dues (tax claims) are also bound by an approved resolution plan.
• Vidarbha Industries remains controversial and has generated debate about whether it gives NCLT excessive discretion, potentially undermining IBC's creditor-friendly design.

concepts_used: Committee of Creditors (CoC): Composition, Voting, and Powers

solution.concept_anchor: CoC — Operational Creditors excluded from voting rights
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both A and R are factually true and see a surface-level connection ('operational creditors are less important → excluded from CoC') may select (a) without recognising that the actual legal rationale for exclusion is the distinct nature of claims, not their relative importance.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Under Section 21(2), only Financial Creditors constitute the CoC; Operational Creditors have no voting rights (only right of representation above a threshold).
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Operational Creditors' claims are for goods/services at agreed prices; they do not bear the risk of the debtor's financial health the way Financial Creditors do.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The legal reason for exclusion per IBC's structure is that Operational Creditors are not exposed to the same credit risk and their claims are more transactional; R describes a true characteristic but it is NOT the operative legal explanation for the CoC composition rule — the Swiss Ribbons case justified it on rational classification, not on 'relative importance.'
Both A and R are correct but R does not correctly explain A → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a classic assertion-reason trap where both statements are independently true but the causal link is wrong. The assertion about CoC composition is a settled legal fact. The reason — that Operational Creditors' claims are transaction-based rather than credit-based — is also a true characterisation. However, it is not the legal rationale embedded in IBC; the Supreme Court in Swiss Ribbons justified the distinction on rational classification grounds. A student who sees both facts as true and assumes causation from correlation will incorrectly select (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The Committee of Creditors is one of IBC's most distinctive innovations — and also one of its most tested features.

Assertion (A): Correct. Under Section 21(2) of IBC, the CoC comprises only Financial Creditors. Operational Creditors have no voting rights; those with claims above a threshold (10% of total debt) may attend CoC meetings and make representations but cannot vote on decisions.

Reason (R): Correct as a factual characterisation. Operational Creditors' claims arise from supply of goods/services — they are essentially trade creditors. Financial Creditors have extended finance and bear credit risk linked to the debtor's solvency. This distinction is factually accurate.

Causal relationship: R does not correctly explain A. The legal basis for excluding Operational Creditors from CoC is not merely that their claims are 'less important' — the IBC design reflects that Financial Creditors, having extended credit, have greater incentive to evaluate resolution plans' economic viability. The Supreme Court in Swiss Ribbons justified this as a reasonable classification, not based on the characterisation offered in R.

Correct option: (b) — Both A and R correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Related party Financial Creditors are excluded from CoC under Section 21(2) — an additional trap dimension.
• Key CoC voting thresholds: 51% for routine decisions; 66% for resolution plan approval, liquidation vote, or replacement of RP.
• The 'commercial wisdom' doctrine prevents courts from substituting their judgment for CoC's on economic decisions.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 53 waterfall mechanism — priority order in liquidation
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students familiar with traditional creditor priority in Indian law (where government dues historically ranked high) often place government dues above unsecured financial creditors, producing the sequence in option (c).
elimination_logic: Anchor on CIRP costs — these always rank first, before any creditor claim. Any option placing them below secured creditors is wrong.
Recall the key IBC reversal: Government dues rank BELOW unsecured financial creditors — this is the defining policy departure from pre-IBC practice.
Workmen dues (24 months) rank with secured creditors in priority, above other employee dues.

The correct sequence is CIRP costs → secured creditors/workmen dues (24 months) → other employee dues → unsecured financial creditors → government dues → remaining secured creditors → equity, pointing to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Government dues ranking below unsecured financial creditors is the single most counterintuitive feature of Section 53. In traditional Indian commercial law and under most pre-IBC frameworks, government claims (tax dues, statutory levies) had priority over most private creditors. IBC deliberately reversed this to make credit more accessible by assuring financial creditors of better recovery — a fundamental policy choice. Students who apply their pre-IBC intuition will rank government dues higher, producing a wrong sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
Section 53 of IBC establishes a statutory waterfall for distribution of proceeds during liquidation — a deliberate departure from traditional priority rules.

The correct order is:
1. CIRP costs and liquidation costs (first charge — always)
2. Secured creditors (who relinquish security) and workmen dues for the preceding 24 months (pari passu)
3. Other employee dues
4. Unsecured Financial Creditors
5. Government dues (Central and State)
6. Remaining secured creditors (who chose to realise outside — their residual claims)
7. Equity shareholders

Option (a): Wrong — places government dues above unsecured financial creditors, which was the pre-IBC position but is explicitly reversed under Section 53.
Option (b): Correct — reflects the precise Section 53 waterfall.
Option (c): Wrong — places employee dues above secured creditors, which is incorrect.
Option (d): Wrong — inverts the entire sequence.

Value Addition:
• The Ghanashyam Mishra case (2021 SC) confirmed that even government tax claims are bound by an approved resolution plan — extending the same logic to the CIRP context.
• Secured creditors have a choice under Section 52: relinquish security to the liquidation estate (and get higher priority) OR realise security outside liquidation (and participate only for residual claims).
• This waterfall applies only in liquidation — during CIRP, CoC determines the distribution through the resolution plan.

concepts_used: Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP): For MSMEs

solution.concept_anchor: PPIRP — debtor-in-possession model for MSMEs
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students aware that CIRP is the standard corporate insolvency process may select it because the scenario involves a company with financial distress, without noting the MSME status and the default range that specifically qualify for PPIRP.
elimination_logic: Note the critical facts: the company is an MSME, the default amount is ₹45 lakh (between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore), and the promoter wants to retain control — these three elements together point exclusively to PPIRP.

Eliminate CIRP (option b): CIRP is creditor-in-control; the promoter loses management. Also, the ₹1 crore CIRP threshold is the minimum — this default of ₹45 lakh is below it for CIRP but within PPIRP range.
Eliminate Voluntary Liquidation (option a): The company is not solvent — it has defaulted on debt and seeks resolution, not winding up.

Eliminate Fast Track CIRP (option c): Fast Track CIRP under Section 55 applies to small companies and start-ups with assets ≤ ₹1 crore but retains the creditor-in-control model, and the promoter still loses management.
Option (d) — PPIRP — is the only mechanism designed for MSMEs with this default range under a debtor-in-possession model.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario is designed to look like a standard CIRP situation. Students who do not know the PPIRP eligibility criteria (MSME + ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore default) or do not remember the debtor-in-possession feature may default to CIRP. The additional nuance is that the CIRP minimum threshold is ₹1 crore — a default of ₹45 lakh falls below it, making CIRP technically inapplicable for this company in the standard route.
solution.final_explanation:
The Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) was introduced through the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2021, specifically for MSMEs facing financial distress.

Applying the facts: Vidyut Components Ltd. is an MSME (registered under MSMED Act), its default is ₹45 lakh (within the ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore window for PPIRP), and the promoter wants to submit a resolution plan before approaching NCLT while retaining operational control. These three elements perfectly match the PPIRP design.

• Option (a) — Voluntary Liquidation: Applicable only when a company is solvent and shareholders decide to wind up. Vidyut is insolvent — this option is inapplicable.
• Option (b) — CIRP: The default threshold for CIRP is ₹1 crore; ₹45 lakh falls below it. Moreover, CIRP follows a creditor-in-control model — the promoter loses management upon NCLT admission.
• Option (c) — Fast Track CIRP: Section 55 covers small companies with assets ≤ ₹1 crore in a 90-day timeline, but it is still creditor-in-control. Promoter retention is not a feature.
• Option (d) — PPIRP: Correct. PPIRP is debtor-in-possession (promoter retains control), designed for MSMEs, applicable for defaults between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore, with a 120-day timeline.

Value Addition:
• PPIRP's Base Resolution Plan must be approved by creditors (66% by value) before the application is filed with NCLT — unlike CIRP where the plan comes after admission.
• PPIRP timeline is 120 days vs. CIRP's 330-day outer limit.
• The debtor-in-possession model reduces the stigma of insolvency for MSME promoters and preserves business relationships.

solution.concept_anchor: Adjudicating authority for personal insolvency — DRT not NCLT
solution.strong_distractor: c — The Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) sounds like it could be an adjudicating authority in personal insolvency, and students who know DRT is involved may confuse DRT with DRAT and select (c) as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify the common category: all options except one should be part of the personal insolvency ecosystem under Part III of IBC.
DRT (Debt Recovery Tribunal) is the adjudicating authority for individuals and partnerships — belongs here.
DRAT (Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal) is the appellate body above DRT in the personal insolvency appeals chain — belongs here.
The Resolution Professional under Part III processes is the insolvency professional for individuals — belongs here.
NCLT (National Company Law Tribunal) adjudicates corporate insolvency (companies and LLPs), NOT personal insolvency — it is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: NCLT is by far the most prominent tribunal in the IBC ecosystem, handling CIRP and liquidation for companies. Students may incorrectly assume it handles all IBC processes. The critical distinction is that Part III of IBC — covering individual and partnership insolvency — designates DRT (not NCLT) as the adjudicating authority. This is a common exam trap because NCLT's dominance in IBC discussions makes it seem universal.
solution.final_explanation:
Part III of IBC creates a separate insolvency architecture for individuals and partnership firms, with the Debt Recovery Tribunal as the adjudicating authority — not NCLT.

• Option (a) — NCLT: This is the odd one out. NCLT adjudicates corporate insolvency (companies and LLPs) under Part II of IBC. For personal insolvency under Part III, DRT is the designated adjudicating authority.
• Option (b) — DRT: Belongs here. Debt Recovery Tribunals are the adjudicating authorities for individual and partnership insolvency under Part III.
• Option (c) — DRAT: Belongs here. Appeals from DRT orders in personal insolvency go to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal.
• Option (d) — Resolution Professional: Belongs here. An insolvency professional acts as Resolution Professional in personal insolvency processes too, managing the process similar to how an RP operates in CIRP.

Value Addition:
• Appeals from NCLT go to NCLAT → Supreme Court; appeals from DRT go to DRAT → High Court → Supreme Court.
• Parts III and IV of IBC (personal insolvency and insolvency of partnership firms) have not been fully operationalised as of recent years — an important examiner's note.
• The Fresh Start Process under Part III applies to individuals with annual income ≤ ₹60,000, assets ≤ ₹20,000, and qualifying debt ≤ ₹35,000.

solution.concept_anchor: NeSL as sole operational IU under IBBI

statement_analysis.statement: National e-Governance Services Ltd. (NeSL) is the only Information Utility currently operational under the regulatory framework of IBBI.
statement_analysis.reason: NeSL received its certificate of registration from IBBI and is the only IU that has become operational — it stores authenticated financial information of debtors accessible to creditors and other stakeholders.

statement_analysis.statement: Information Utilities under IBC are required to store financial information only for Corporate Debtors undergoing active CIRP proceedings, and their services are not available during the pre-insolvency stage.
statement_analysis.reason: IUs store financial information proactively — lenders are required to submit credit information on an ongoing basis, not merely when insolvency is triggered. The purpose is to reduce information asymmetry before and during insolvency, enabling faster claims verification upon initiation of CIRP.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know NeSL is the only operational IU and also believe IUs are triggered only during insolvency (a plausible but wrong inference) may mark both statements as correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: NeSL is indeed the only IU that has received IBBI registration and become operational — Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: IUs are designed for continuous pre-insolvency data submission by lenders — they are NOT restricted to active CIRP cases. The restriction described in Statement 2 does not exist in IBC; it contradicts the purpose of reducing information asymmetry proactively.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The fabricated restriction in Statement 2 — that IUs operate only during active CIRP — sounds logical to someone who connects IUs with the insolvency process. In reality, IUs are designed to be repositories of financial information submitted by financial creditors on an ongoing basis, making them available immediately when insolvency is triggered, thereby speeding up the CIRP timeline. The trap exploits the intuitive but incorrect assumption that insolvency infrastructure is activated only when insolvency begins.
solution.final_explanation:
Information Utilities (IUs) are a foundational element of IBC's information architecture, designed to address the pervasive information asymmetry in India's credit markets.

• Statement 1 — Correct: NeSL (National e-Governance Services Ltd.) is the only IU that has received IBBI registration and become operational. It holds authenticated records of financial contracts between borrowers and lenders.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: IUs are not limited to active insolvency cases. Financial creditors are required to submit financial information to IUs continuously. When a CIRP is triggered, this pre-stored data enables rapid claims verification — cutting weeks from the process. There is no restriction to 'active CIRP only.'

Value Addition:
• IBBI regulates IUs under Section 210 of IBC — covering registration, data standards, and access norms.
• The primary benefit of IUs: authenticated data submitted by the creditor at the time of lending prevents debtors from later disputing the existence or quantum of debt.
• IUs reduce fraudulent claims in insolvency proceedings — a key reform objective alongside speed and transparency.

solution.concept_anchor: Three recognized IPAs and their parent institutions
solution.strong_distractor: c — IBBI itself regulates IPAs, so students may confuse the regulator of IPAs with the list of IPAs, assuming IBBI directly enrolls IPs rather than delegating that function to IPAs.
elimination_logic: Recall that IPAs are Self-Regulatory Organizations — they enroll and regulate individual Insolvency Professionals.
Three bodies are recognized as IPAs: one under ICSI (ICSI-IIP), one promoted by IBA (IIIPI), and one under ICAI (ICAI-IIP) — all membership-based professional bodies.
The IBA-promoted IPA is IIIPI (Indian Institute of Insolvency Professionals of ICAI — wait: IIIPI is promoted by IBA; ICAI-IIP is under ICAI).
The correct triple is ICSI-IIP, IIIPI, and ICAI-IIP → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here is between IBBI (the regulator) and IPAs (the self-regulatory bodies). Students know IBBI regulates the insolvency ecosystem and may conflate IBBI's regulatory role with the enrollment/registration function that IPAs perform. Additionally, the three IPAs — two linked to premier professional bodies (ICAI and ICSI) and one to IBA — look deceptively similar, making it easy to mistake one for another or to substitute a plausible-sounding body.
solution.final_explanation:
Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPAs) are Self-Regulatory Organizations under IBBI that enroll, regulate, and discipline individual Insolvency Professionals — creating a two-tier regulatory architecture.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: This combination includes a fictitious 'IBBI-IPA' — IBBI itself is the apex regulator, not an IPA. IBBI regulates IPAs; it does not function as one.
• Option (b) — Correct: The three recognized IPAs are ICSI-IIP (under the Institute of Company Secretaries of India), IIIPI (Indian Institute of Insolvency Professionals of ICAI, promoted by the Indian Banks' Association), and ICAI-IIP (under the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Substitutes IBBI for one of the actual IPAs — a direct conflation of regulator and regulated.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Replaces ICSI-IIP with a fabricated 'ICWAI-IIP' — the Institute of Cost Accountants is not among the recognized IPAs.

Value Addition:
• IPAs → IPs: Two-tier architecture — IBBI regulates IPAs; IPAs enroll and discipline IPs.
• An insolvency professional must be enrolled with one IPA to practice.
• The distinction between IPA (institutional SRO) and IP (individual professional) is a common exam confusion point.

solution.concept_anchor: Appeals hierarchy — NCLT vs. DRT chains under IBC
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know NCLAT is above NCLT may select (b) as 'correctly matched,' not noticing that (b) places High Court above NCLAT in the NCLT appeals chain — which is wrong (appeals from NCLAT go to the Supreme Court, not the High Court).
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The appeals chain from DRT goes to DRAT, not NCLAT — NCLAT is specific to the corporate insolvency (NCLT) chain.
Eliminate (b): From NCLAT, appeals go to the Supreme Court (on a question of law) — not to the High Court. This pair swaps High Court for Supreme Court.
Eliminate (c): IBBI is a regulatory body, not an appellate authority — it has no role in hearing appeals from NCLT orders. This is a fabricated pair.
Confirm (d): DRT → DRAT → High Court → Supreme Court is the correct appellate chain for personal insolvency proceedings under Part III of IBC.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The appeals hierarchy question exploits two traps simultaneously. First, students may confuse the NCLT chain (NCLT → NCLAT → Supreme Court) with the DRT chain (DRT → DRAT → High Court → Supreme Court). Second, the insertion of 'High Court' in the NCLT chain (option b) sounds plausible because High Courts have supervisory jurisdiction over tribunals under Article 227, making it a conceptually attractive but legally wrong distractor in the IBC appeals context.
solution.final_explanation:
IBC establishes two parallel adjudicatory systems with separate appeals hierarchies.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: DRT appeals go to DRAT, not NCLAT. NCLAT is the appellate body for NCLT — these chains do not cross.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: NCLT appeals go to NCLAT, and from NCLAT to the Supreme Court (only on a question of law) — High Court is not in this chain.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: IBBI is purely a regulatory body — it has no appellate function. Appeals from NCLT orders go to NCLAT, never to IBBI.
• Option (d) — Correct: For personal insolvency (individuals and partnership firms) under Part III of IBC, the adjudicating authority is DRT. Appeals from DRT go to DRAT (Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal), then to the High Court, and finally to the Supreme Court.

Value Addition:
• The NCLT chain: NCLT → NCLAT → Supreme Court (question of law only).
• The DRT chain (personal insolvency): DRT → DRAT → High Court → Supreme Court.
• IBBI cannot hear appeals — it is a regulatory and quasi-judicial disciplinary body, not an appellate tribunal.

concepts_used: Cross-Border Insolvency: UNCITRAL Model Law and India's Position

solution.concept_anchor: India's cross-border insolvency position — UNCITRAL Model Law not adopted

statement_analysis.statement: India has formally adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency 1997, incorporating its provisions into the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code through the 2021 amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: As of the available knowledge, India has NOT adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law. The Insolvency Law Committee (2018) recommended its adoption with modifications, but the recommendation has not been legislatively implemented.

statement_analysis.statement: Sections 234 and 235 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code enable the Central Government to enter into bilateral agreements with other countries to resolve cross-border insolvency matters.
statement_analysis.reason: Sections 234 and 235 provide the existing mechanism — Section 234 for bilateral treaties with foreign nations, and Section 235 for seeking assistance from foreign courts — though neither has been operationalized through actual treaties.

statement_analysis.statement: The concept of 'Centre of Main Interests' (COMI) is a key principle in the UNCITRAL Model Law framework for determining which jurisdiction's insolvency proceedings should be recognised as the primary proceedings.
statement_analysis.reason: COMI is the foundational concept in the UNCITRAL Model Law — it determines the 'home country' of the debtor's main business operations, and that jurisdiction's proceedings receive primary recognition under the modified universalism approach.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who have read about IBC amendments and know PPIRP was introduced in 2021 may incorrectly assume cross-border insolvency provisions were also formally enacted in 2021, making 'all three' statements appear correct.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Statement 1 as correct — India has NOT adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law despite the 2018 Insolvency Law Committee recommendation; confusing a committee recommendation with legislative enactment is the classic trap.
Confirm Statement 2 — Sections 234 and 235 exist in the current IBC text as the existing (though underutilized) cross-border framework.
Confirm Statement 3 — COMI is the defining principle of the UNCITRAL Model Law's modified universalism approach.
Statements 2 and 3 correct, Statement 1 incorrect → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap is attributing the UNCITRAL Model Law adoption to the 2021 IBC amendment. The 2021 amendment introduced PPIRP — a highly publicised reform. Students who know of significant IBC changes in 2021 may assume cross-border provisions were also enacted then. The reality is that Sections 234 and 235 exist as framework provisions but bilateral agreements have not been signed, and the full UNCITRAL Model Law has not been adopted — a distinction between framework existence and operationalization.
solution.final_explanation:
Cross-border insolvency is an area where IBC's framework exists on paper but lacks full operationalization.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: India has not adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency 1997. The Insolvency Law Committee (2018) recommended adoption with India-specific modifications, but no legislative amendment has implemented this recommendation. The 2021 IBC amendment introduced PPIRP — not cross-border insolvency provisions.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Sections 234 and 235 of IBC provide the existing bilateral agreement mechanism. However, no bilateral treaties have been operationalised under these provisions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Centre of Main Interests (COMI) principle — where a debtor's primary business interests are located — determines which country's insolvency proceedings get primary recognition under the UNCITRAL Model Law's modified universalism framework.

Statements 2 and 3 correct → option (b).

Value Addition:
• 'Modified universalism' (UNCITRAL's approach) sits between strict territorialism (each country handles its own assets) and full universalism (one court handles all global assets).
• India's absence from the UNCITRAL framework creates problems for cross-border resolution of large conglomerates like IL&FS which had international exposures.
• The Insolvency Law Committee also recommended a COMI-based approach for India — indicating alignment in principle even without formal adoption.

solution.concept_anchor: IBC moratorium overrides SARFAESI; both laws coexist

statement_analysis.statement: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, expressly repealed the SARFAESI Act, 2002, replacing it entirely as the primary statute for secured creditor enforcement.
statement_analysis.reason: IBC did NOT repeal SARFAESI. Both laws coexist. SARFAESI remains operational for individual secured creditor enforcement outside insolvency; IBC overrides SARFAESI enforcement only during the Section 14 moratorium period.

statement_analysis.statement: During the moratorium declared under Section 14 of IBC, enforcement actions initiated by a secured creditor under the SARFAESI Act against the Corporate Debtor's assets are stayed.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 14 moratorium prohibits all enforcement actions against the Corporate Debtor's assets, including SARFAESI enforcement — this is explicitly stated in IBC and was the subject of multiple judicial pronouncements.

statement_analysis.statement: Under IBC, a secured creditor in liquidation must relinquish its security interest to the liquidation estate and cannot realise the security outside the liquidation proceedings.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 52 of IBC gives a secured creditor a choice: relinquish the security interest to the liquidation estate and participate in the waterfall, OR realize the security outside the liquidation process independently. The mandatory relinquishment described in Statement 3 does not exist.

solution.strong_distractor: c — A student who believes SARFAESI was repealed (Statement 1 incorrect — correctly identified) but also incorrectly believes the moratorium only stays court proceedings and not SARFAESI actions (thus marking Statement 2 as also incorrect) will select (c), when in fact only Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect.
elimination_logic: Identify Statement 1 as incorrect — IBC did not repeal SARFAESI; both coexist, with IBC overriding SARFAESI only during the moratorium.
Identify Statement 2 as correct — Section 14 moratorium explicitly stays SARFAESI enforcement against the corporate debtor.
Identify Statement 3 as incorrect — Section 52 gives secured creditors a choice between relinquishing security or realizing outside liquidation; there is no mandatory relinquishment.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct; the question asks which are not correct → option that includes '1 and 3 only' = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 3 adds 'cannot' to convert a discretionary provision into a mandatory prohibition. Section 52 explicitly gives the secured creditor an election — a key creditor-friendly design feature of IBC's liquidation framework. Students who know that SARFAESI enforcement is stayed during moratorium may also incorrectly generalise this stay into the liquidation phase, assuming secured creditors always lose their individual enforcement rights under IBC.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between IBC and SARFAESI is one of coexistence, not replacement — a critical distinction tested repeatedly.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: IBC did not repeal SARFAESI. SARFAESI remains operative for secured creditor enforcement outside insolvency. IBC overrides SARFAESI only when Section 14 moratorium is in effect.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Section 14 moratorium expressly prohibits all enforcement actions against the Corporate Debtor — including those initiated under SARFAESI. Secured creditors must pause their enforcement once NCLT admits the CIRP application.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Section 52 provides secured creditors with an explicit choice in liquidation: either relinquish the security interest to the liquidation estate (and get priority in the waterfall) OR realize the security independently outside the liquidation process. Mandatory relinquishment is a fabrication.

Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct → option (b).

Value Addition:
• SARFAESI is generally faster for a single secured creditor pursuing one borrower — IBC is more appropriate when multiple creditors are involved.
• SARFAESI minimum debt threshold: ₹1 lakh; IBC CIRP threshold: ₹1 crore for companies.
• Secured creditors who realise security outside liquidation must contribute any excess recovery to the liquidation estate.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 29A eligibility — ineligibility criteria for resolution applicants

statement_analysis.statement: A person who is a wilful defaulter as classified by any scheduled commercial bank is ineligible to submit a resolution plan under Section 29A of IBC.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 29A(b) explicitly disqualifies wilful defaulters — those classified as such by any scheduled commercial bank or financial institution — from acting as resolution applicants.

statement_analysis.statement: Section 29A disqualifies a resolution applicant whose accounts have been classified as Non-Performing Assets for a period of one year or more.
statement_analysis.reason: The NPA disqualification under Section 29A requires that the account be NPA for one year or more AND that the applicant has failed to make the outstanding payment — but the period is one year, not 'more than one year.' However, the Supreme Court in Arcelormittal held this disqualification applies even if the NPA is in the name of a connected person, not just the applicant directly. The statement as worded ('one year or more') is actually correct in the basic threshold — re-evaluating: Section 29A(c) disqualifies those whose accounts were NPA for one year or more. Statement is Correct.

statement_analysis.statement: A resolution applicant who has been convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for two years or more under any law is ineligible under Section 29A.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 29A(d) disqualifies persons convicted of any offence punishable with two or more years of imprisonment under specified laws — this is a broad disqualification covering criminal convictions beyond just financial crimes.

statement_analysis.statement: Once a resolution plan is approved by the Committee of Creditors and the NCLT, it becomes binding only on the Corporate Debtor and the Financial Creditors who voted in its favour, and not on dissenting creditors or government authorities.
statement_analysis.reason: Per IBC Section 31 and as upheld in Ghanashyam Mishra (2021), an NCLT-approved resolution plan is binding on ALL stakeholders — including dissenting creditors, Operational Creditors, and Central/State government dues.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct but mistakenly recall the NPA disqualification period as 'more than one year' (making Statement 2 incorrect) would arrive at 'only two' (Statements 1 and 3), selecting (b) — not (c). The trap is layered.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 as correct — wilful defaulters are expressly disqualified under Section 29A(b).
Confirm Statement 2 as correct — Section 29A(c) disqualifies those with NPA accounts for one year or more; the wording 'one year or more' matches the statutory text.
Confirm Statement 3 as correct — conviction for offences punishable with two or more years imprisonment is a disqualification under Section 29A(d).
Identify Statement 4 as incorrect — an approved resolution plan binds ALL stakeholders including dissenting creditors and government dues per Section 31 and Supreme Court jurisprudence.
Three statements correct (1, 2, 3) → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is the precision trap — the 'binding only on those who voted in favour' formulation sounds fair and democratic but is factually wrong. IBC's design requires the resolution plan to bind all — including government tax authorities and dissenting creditors — because any carve-out would allow holdouts to derail the plan. Students who apply general contract law intuition (you are bound only if you agreed) fail here.
solution.final_explanation:
Section 29A and Section 31 are two of IBC's most examined provisions.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 1. Wilful defaulters ineligible under S.29A | Correct |
| 2. NPA for one year or more — ineligible | Correct |
| 3. Convicted of offence (2+ years) — ineligible | Correct |
| 4. Approved plan binds only consenting creditors | Incorrect |

Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct; Statement 4 is incorrect because Section 31 makes the approved resolution plan binding on the corporate debtor, all creditors (including dissenting), all employees, and government authorities — as confirmed in Ghanashyam Mishra (2021). Three correct → option (c).

Value Addition:
• Section 29A's 'connected persons' disqualification extends to persons acting in concert, related parties, and holding/subsidiary companies — Arcelormittal case strictly interpreted this.
• A resolution applicant who was previously ineligible can become eligible by clearing NPA dues before submitting the resolution plan.
• The binding nature of the approved plan over government dues was critical to resolving large stressed assets like Bhushan Steel.

concepts_used: Insolvency Resolution Professional (IRP) and Resolution Professional (RP): Roles and Accountability

solution.concept_anchor: Board of Directors suspension upon RP taking over — Section 17
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the CoC has the power to 'replace' the IRP may incorrectly recall the vote threshold as 51% (routine majority) rather than 66% (special resolution for key decisions like RP replacement).
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): NCLT does not 'suspend' the Board — it is the appointment of the IRP/RP that triggers suspension under Section 17; NCLT's role is admission of the application.
Eliminate (b): The CoC can replace the IRP with an RP of its choice — but this requires a 66% vote, not a simple 51% majority.
Eliminate (c): The RP manages the company as a going concern — the Board is suspended, not merely 'advisory.' Directors lose all management powers.

Confirm (d): Section 17 of IBC is explicit — upon appointment of the IRP, the powers of the Board of Directors vest in the IRP/RP, and the Board stands suspended. This is the 'creditor-in-control' feature of CIRP.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in option (b) replaces the correct threshold (66%) with the plausible but wrong 51%. Since 51% is the threshold for routine CoC decisions, a partially prepared student will see '51%' as familiar and credible. The critical discipline is remembering that replacement of the IRP — a key decision — requires the 66% supermajority like resolution plan approval and liquidation votes.
solution.final_explanation:
The Resolution Professional's assumption of management powers is a defining feature of IBC's CIRP architecture.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: NCLT's role upon admission is to appoint the IRP and declare the moratorium — the suspension of the Board is a consequence of the IRP's appointment under Section 17, not a direct NCLT order of suspension.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The CoC can replace the IRP with its preferred RP, but only by a 66% vote — not 51%. The 51% threshold applies to routine operational decisions.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Board of Directors is not merely 'downgraded to advisory' — it is fully suspended. All management powers vest in the IRP/RP during CIRP.
• Option (d) — Correct: Section 17 of IBC provides that on the insolvency commencement date, the management of the corporate debtor vests in the IRP, and the Board's powers stand suspended. Directors can be removed and the RP acts as de facto management.

Value Addition:
• The IRP is initially appointed by NCLT; the CoC can then replace the IRP with an RP of its choice (66% vote).
• The RP must function as a going concern — maintaining operations, paying salaries, and keeping the business alive during CIRP.
• IBBI's disciplinary jurisdiction over IPs includes this phase — an RP who mismanages during CIRP can face inspection and penalty.

solution.concept_anchor: Voluntary Liquidation — solvency requirement; not an insolvency process

statement_analysis.statement: Voluntary Liquidation under Section 59 of IBC can be initiated by a solvent company whose shareholders wish to wind up operations, and requires a declaration that the company is able to pay its debts in full.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 59 is explicitly for solvent companies — the board must make a declaration of solvency (that the company can pay its debts within 12 months) and shareholders must pass a resolution. This is fundamentally NOT an insolvency process.

statement_analysis.statement: The Fast Track Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 55 of IBC applies to all companies with outstanding debt below ₹1 crore, irrespective of their listing status or age of incorporation.
statement_analysis.reason: Fast Track CIRP under Section 55 applies to specific categories: small companies, start-up companies (less than 2 years old), and unlisted companies with total assets not exceeding ₹1 crore — it is category-specific, not a universal threshold-based provision applying to all companies with debt below ₹1 crore.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the ₹1 crore threshold for CIRP and the Fast Track CIRP's existence may conflate the CIRP threshold with the Fast Track eligibility criterion, assuming Statement 2 correctly describes a debt-based threshold.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Voluntary Liquidation under Section 59 requires solvency declaration — correct. It is for companies choosing to wind up, not for insolvent companies. Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: Fast Track CIRP eligibility is category-based (small companies, startups <2 years, unlisted with assets ≤ ₹1 crore) — not a universal 'debt below ₹1 crore' rule. The statement incorrectly universalises a category-specific provision. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in Statement 2 merges the Fast Track CIRP eligibility criteria with the regular CIRP threshold. The ₹1 crore figure appears in both contexts (CIRP minimum threshold and Fast Track asset ceiling) but means different things — one is about the minimum default to trigger CIRP; the other is an asset ceiling for one of the eligible categories in Fast Track. A student who recognises the ₹1 crore number as 'correct' without parsing its meaning in each context will mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Both Voluntary Liquidation and Fast Track CIRP are alternative processes under IBC — each with distinct eligibility logic.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 59 Voluntary Liquidation is available only to solvent companies. The process begins with a board declaration of solvency (ability to pay all debts within 12 months), followed by a shareholder resolution. This is a winding-up choice for a financially healthy company — fundamentally different from insolvency resolution.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Fast Track CIRP under Section 55 is category-specific. Eligible companies are: (i) small companies as defined under the Companies Act, (ii) start-up companies less than 2 years old, and (iii) unlisted companies with total assets not exceeding ₹1 crore. The statement's claim that it applies to 'all companies with debt below ₹1 crore irrespective of status or age' overgeneralises the provision incorrectly.

Value Addition:
• Fast Track CIRP timeline: 90 days (extendable by 45 days) vs. regular CIRP's 330-day outer limit.
• IBBI data shows very low uptake of Fast Track CIRP in practice — a likely awareness-testing fact for examiners.
• Voluntary Liquidation ≠ Insolvency: A company voluntarily liquidating has no creditor dispute and no financial distress — the liquidator distributes assets to shareholders after paying all creditors.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional backing — Entry 9, Concurrent List for insolvency
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that banking and company law are Union List subjects may incorrectly classify insolvency under the Union List, particularly because NCLT (a central tribunal) and IBBI (a central body) administer IBC.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Insolvency is not in the Union List — checking Entry 9 in the Concurrent List confirms it is a shared subject, not exclusive to the Centre.
Eliminate (c): The State List does not include insolvency — states cannot independently legislate on corporate insolvency.
Eliminate (d): There is no 'Residuary List' in the Indian Constitution — residuary powers vest in Parliament under Article 248, but insolvency is specifically listed in the Concurrent List.
Confirm (b): Entry 9 of the Concurrent List (Schedule VII) covers 'Bankruptcy and insolvency' — both Centre and States can legislate, but Parliament's law prevails under Article 254.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap here operates within the three lists — students who associate IBC's central administration with Union List jurisdiction make a structural error. The Centre administers IBC with overriding authority under Article 254(2), but the constitutional home of insolvency is Entry 9 in the Concurrent List. This distinction matters because it opens the door for states to enact complementary legislation — a theoretical possibility that also tests constitutional literacy.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional basis of IBC is a foundational but frequently overlooked dimension of its legislative framework.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Union List (List I) does not contain insolvency. Subjects like banking (Entry 45) and corporations (Entry 43) are in the Union List, making this a plausible but wrong answer.
• Option (b) — Correct: Entry 9 of the Concurrent List reads 'Bankruptcy and insolvency' — this is the constitutional hook for IBC. Both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate on this subject, but Parliamentary law prevails in case of repugnancy (Article 254).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The State List does not include insolvency. States cannot independently create insolvency tribunals or processes.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Indian Constitution has no 'Residuary List.' Residuary powers vest in Parliament under Article 248, but insolvency is specifically enumerated in the Concurrent List.

Value Addition:
• Article 254(1): If state law conflicts with central law on a Concurrent List subject, central law prevails to the extent of repugnancy.
• The Centre's overriding jurisdiction through IBC effectively makes insolvency a central subject in practice despite its Concurrent List status.
• Entry 43 (Union List): Incorporation of companies — distinct from insolvency; companies are a Union subject but their insolvency is a Concurrent subject.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

(a) The Union List, as Parliament has exclusive legislative competence over all corporate financial matters
(b) The Concurrent List, though Parliament's law prevails over any State legislation on the subject
(c) The State List, enabling states to legislate on insolvency with Parliament's assent
(d) The Residuary List, as insolvency was not anticipated by the Constitution's framers

solution.concept_anchor: Section 14 moratorium — what is stayed vs. what continues

statement_analysis.statement: During the Section 14 moratorium under IBC, the supply of essential goods and services to the Corporate Debtor cannot be terminated or suspended.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 14(2) of IBC explicitly protects essential goods and services — suppliers cannot cut off supply to the corporate debtor during the moratorium, ensuring the business continues as a going concern.

statement_analysis.statement: The Section 14 moratorium prohibits the institution of all legal proceedings against the Corporate Debtor, including criminal proceedings initiated by regulatory authorities.
statement_analysis.reason: The moratorium under Section 14 covers civil suits, execution proceedings, asset transfers, and security enforcement — it does NOT stay criminal proceedings. Regulatory enforcement actions of a criminal nature are outside the moratorium's scope.

statement_analysis.statement: The outer time limit for completing the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, including time spent in litigation, was set at 330 days by an amendment to IBC.
statement_analysis.reason: The IBC (Amendment) Act, 2019 inserted the mandatory outer limit of 330 days for completion of CIRP including judicial proceedings — beyond this, NCLT must pass a liquidation order. This replaced the earlier practice-based extensions.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know the moratorium is broad and protective may assume it covers ALL proceedings including criminal — especially because regulatory bodies like SEBI or ED may be pursuing the same corporate debtor for fraud. The 'all proceedings' scope-extension in Statement 2 feels protective and logical.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 as correct — Section 14(2) specifically carves out essential goods and services from the moratorium's reach, ensuring supply continues.
Identify Statement 2 as incorrect — criminal proceedings are NOT stayed by the Section 14 moratorium; the moratorium is civil in character and covers suits, asset transfers, and enforcement actions.
Confirm Statement 3 as correct — the 330-day mandatory outer limit including litigation time was introduced by the 2019 amendment.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 adds 'including criminal proceedings' to the moratorium's reach. The moratorium is intentionally designed for civil enforcement — it prevents the race among creditors to grab assets. Criminal proceedings against promoters or directors (e.g., ED investigations, SFIO cases) are expressly outside its scope. Students who appreciate the moratorium's broad protective purpose may intuitively accept the extension to criminal proceedings without recalling the statutory limitation.
solution.final_explanation:
The Section 14 moratorium is the immediate protective shield that makes CIRP viable — but its scope is defined, not unlimited.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 14(2) ensures essential goods and services cannot be cut off during the moratorium. This is critical — without power, water, or raw materials, the business cannot operate as a going concern, destroying the value that creditors seek to recover.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The moratorium covers civil suits, execution of judgments, asset transfers, and enforcement actions (including SARFAESI). Criminal proceedings — whether by ED, SFIO, or state police — are NOT stayed. Promoters can continue to face criminal action even while CIRP proceeds.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 2019 amendment introduced the mandatory 330-day ceiling — original timeline was 180 days + 90 days extension (270 days), but courts were granting further extensions. The 330-day hard deadline was meant to restore time discipline.

Value Addition:
• The 330-day limit includes time spent in litigation at NCLT, NCLAT, and Supreme Court — not just the resolution process itself.
• Post-moratorium, if no plan is approved within 330 days, NCLT must order liquidation.
• Section 14(2A) — added by 2018 amendment — clarifies that a licensor cannot terminate a licence or permit of the corporate debtor during the moratorium.

solution.concept_anchor: FSPs excluded from regular IBC — Section 227 special rules
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both A and R are true and see a surface connection ('FSPs need special rules' → 'therefore special regulator involvement is the reason') may select (a), missing that R describes a consequence/feature of FSP rules rather than the causal reason for their exclusion from regular IBC.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Banks, NBFCs, insurance companies (Financial Service Providers) are not subject to regular IBC CIRP. Section 227 empowers the government to notify special insolvency rules for FSPs.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. When an FSP undergoes insolvency, the relevant sector regulator (RBI for banks/NBFCs, IRDAI for insurers, SEBI for market entities) is involved in nominating or concurring on the administrator.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. FSPs are excluded from regular IBC primarily because of their systemic importance, the risk of depositor/policyholder runs, and the need for sector-specific resolution tools — NOT primarily because their regulators are involved in nomination. Regulator involvement is a design feature of FSP resolution, not the cause of their exclusion from regular IBC.
Both A and R correct, but R does not correctly explain A → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap presents regulator involvement in FSP insolvency (a true feature) as the cause of FSP exclusion from regular IBC (also true but for different reasons). The actual causes of FSP exclusion are systemic risk, depositor protection, and the need for continuity of financial services — these are the rationale. Regulator involvement is how FSP resolution is designed, not why FSPs are excluded. A student who finds both A and R factually true and sees a plausible (but incorrect) causal chain will select (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The resolution of Financial Service Providers under IBC is a structurally distinct regime designed to address the unique risks posed by financial institutions.

Assertion (A): Correct. Banks, NBFCs, insurance companies, and other Financial Service Providers are NOT subject to the regular CIRP under IBC. Section 227 of IBC empowers the Central Government (in consultation with financial sector regulators) to notify special rules for insolvency of FSPs. The IBC (Insolvency and Liquidation Proceedings of Financial Service Providers and Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules 2019 were framed under this provision.

Reason (R): Correct as a factual description. When an FSP undergoes insolvency under Section 227 rules, an Administrator (not RP) is appointed, and the relevant sectoral regulator (RBI for banks/NBFCs, IRDAI for insurers) nominates or concurs on this appointment.

Causal relationship: R does not correctly explain A. FSPs are excluded from regular IBC because of systemic risk concerns, the public interest in continuity of financial services, and the risk of depositor/policyholder panic — not merely because their regulators need to be involved in nomination. Regulator involvement is a consequence of the special regime, not its cause.

Correct option: (b)

Value Addition:
• The FRDI Bill 2017 (Financial Resolution and Deposit Insurance Bill) was withdrawn amid public controversy over the 'bail-in' clause — it would have replaced depositor protection with a resolution fund.
• IL&FS, DHFL, and Yes Bank resolutions each used different mechanisms (IBC FSP rules, RBI-led intervention, and amalgamation scheme respectively), highlighting regulatory gaps.
• DICI (Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation) insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank — a key consumer protection complementing FSP resolution.

Reason (R): When a Financial Service Provider undergoes insolvency proceedings under these special rules, the relevant sectoral regulator — such as the Reserve Bank of India or the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority — is involved in the nomination or concurrence of the administrator appointed to manage the financial institution.

solution.concept_anchor: IBBI disciplinary process — three-stage inspection, investigation, adjudication
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know investigation follows inspection may swap the adjudication and investigation stages, placing penalty imposition (adjudication) before formal investigation completes — a logical but incorrect ordering.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Inspection as the first stage — IBBI conducts inspection of the IP's records and conduct before any formal action; this is the information-gathering phase.
Investigation follows inspection when inspection reveals potential violations — an Investigating Authority is appointed under Section 218 to conduct a formal inquiry.
Adjudication before the Adjudicating Officer (within IBBI) occurs after investigation findings are submitted — this is the quasi-judicial phase where the IP gets a hearing.
Penalty/disciplinary order is the outcome of adjudication — it comes last. Correct sequence: Inspection → Investigation → Adjudication (hearing) → Penalty Order → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The sequence trap here is between investigation and adjudication. Students who know that penalties are imposed at the end may correctly place the penalty order last, but then incorrectly swap investigation and adjudication in the middle stages — especially because 'adjudication' sounds like it should come before 'investigation' in colloquial understanding (one 'adjudicates' to decide whether to investigate). In regulatory law, investigation is always the fact-finding stage before the quasi-judicial hearing (adjudication).
solution.final_explanation:
IBBI's enforcement process follows a structured three-stage sequence designed to protect due process while maintaining regulatory discipline over insolvency professionals.

Correct sequence:
1. Inspection: IBBI or its authorised officer inspects the IP's records, processes, and conduct — either suo motu or on complaint. This is non-adversarial information collection.
2. Investigation: If inspection reveals material violations, a formal investigation is ordered under Section 218. An Investigating Authority is appointed, examines records, and submits a report.
3. Adjudication: The Adjudicating Officer within IBBI conducts a quasi-judicial hearing — the IP gets an opportunity to be heard. This maintains separation of functions (investigation ≠ adjudication).
4. Penalty/Disciplinary Order: The outcome — which may be a warning, suspension, cancellation of registration, or monetary penalty (up to ₹1 crore or 3x illegal gains).

Option (c) — Inspection → Investigation → Adjudication → Penalty — is the correct sequence.

Value Addition:
• IBBI's Adjudicating Officer mechanism ensures the investigator and adjudicator are different officials — a due process safeguard.
• Monetary penalty ceiling: ₹1 crore OR three times the amount of profits made through the contravention, whichever is higher.
• IBBI can also initiate action suo motu without a complaint — an important regulatory power distinguishing it from passive bodies.

solution.concept_anchor: Government dues below unsecured financial creditors in Section 53 waterfall
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) states that government dues rank above unsecured financial creditors — this was the traditional legal position under pre-IBC law and remains the intuitive default for students who haven't memorised the Section 53 waterfall reversal.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): 'Workmen dues for 36 months' is incorrect — Section 53 specifies workmen dues for the preceding 24 months, pari passu with secured creditors who relinquish security.
Eliminate (b): Government dues ranking above unsecured financial creditors is the pre-IBC position — IBC reversed this; government dues now rank below unsecured financial creditors in Section 53.
Eliminate (c): 'Resolution Costs rank below secured creditors' is wrong — CIRP and liquidation costs are first in the waterfall, above all creditors.
Confirm (d): A secured creditor in liquidation has the express right under Section 52 to realise its security outside the liquidation process — this is a correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) exploits historical legal intuition — the idea that the government (tax authority, labour boards) has priority over private creditors was enshrined in pre-IBC law. IBC's deliberate policy reversal — placing government dues below unsecured financial creditors — was one of its most debated provisions. Students who have not specifically studied Section 53 will revert to this pre-IBC intuition and incorrectly select (b) as 'correctly matched.'
solution.final_explanation:
Section 53's waterfall mechanism represents one of IBC's most significant policy reversals from traditional Indian commercial law.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: 'Workmen dues for 36 months' is a wrong figure. Section 53(1)(b)(ii) specifies workmen dues for the preceding 24 months — not 36.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Government dues (Central and State tax claims) rank BELOW unsecured financial creditors in the Section 53 waterfall. This reversal from pre-IBC priority is intentional — to make credit extension more attractive by assuring financial creditors of better recovery.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: CIRP costs and liquidation costs are the first charge on liquidation proceeds — they rank above all creditors including secured creditors.
• Option (d) — Correct: Section 52 gives a secured creditor the explicit right to either relinquish its security interest to the liquidation estate (and participate in the waterfall) OR realise the security outside the liquidation process independently.

Value Addition:
• If a secured creditor realises security outside liquidation and recovers more than its due, the excess must be contributed to the liquidation estate.
• The government dues reversal was upheld by the Supreme Court in Ghanashyam Mishra — the state cannot claim priority in insolvency that Parliament has denied.
• CIRP costs include the IRP/RP's fees, which rank first — incentivising professionals to take up assignments.
