solution.concept_anchor: Homebuyers as Financial Creditors — Section 7 filing rights
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know homebuyers have rights under IBC but are uncertain whether they file under Section 7 or Section 9 may select option (c) which places them under Section 9 as Operational Creditors — a category that sounds 'operational' and transactional, fitting a purchase transaction.
elimination_logic: Identify the homebuyers' legal status: Per the 2018 IBC amendment, allottees of real estate projects are classified as Financial Creditors — their advance payments constitute financial debt under Section 5(8)(f).
As Financial Creditors, they file under Section 7 — not Section 9 (which is for Operational Creditors).
Eliminate (a): Homebuyers cannot file under Section 9 — Operational Creditor status requires a claim for goods/services at an agreed price, not a loan/advance.

Eliminate (c): Homebuyers cannot form an independent CoC — the CoC comprises Financial Creditors with admitted claims post-CIRP admission; homebuyers participate as members of the CoC alongside banks.
Eliminate (d): Homebuyers do not approach DRT — DRT is for individual/partnership insolvency. The builder is a company; NCLT is the forum.
Confirm (b): Homebuyers (minimum 100 or 10% of allottees, whichever is less) can jointly file under Section 7 before NCLT as Financial Creditors.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap places homebuyers under Section 9 (Operational Creditor route) — which is deceptively plausible because a home purchase feels like a 'transaction for goods' (purchasing an apartment). The critical legal distinction is that advance payment by a homebuyer creates a financial debt (money raised against a promise to deliver an asset) — making it a financial debt, not an operational one. The Chitra Sharma case and subsequent 2018 amendment crystallised this classification.
solution.final_explanation:
After the 2018 IBC amendment and the Supreme Court's validation, homebuyers have a defined legal standing in builder insolvency cases.

Applying the facts: Shivam Residences is a company (CIRP forum is NCLT). The allottees paid advances — these are financial debts under Section 5(8)(f) as amended in 2018. As Financial Creditors, their recourse is Section 7 filing.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Section 9 is for Operational Creditors — those supplying goods or services. A homebuyer's advance is a financial debt, not an operational claim.
• Option (b) — Correct: Homebuyers, classified as Financial Creditors since the 2018 amendment, can jointly file an application under Section 7 before the NCLT. To prevent individual filings overwhelming the system, at least 100 allottees or 10% of allottees (whichever is less) must join the application.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Homebuyers do not form a separate CoC. They participate in the existing CoC alongside banks and financial institutions as Financial Creditors — the CoC is a single body.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: DRT is the adjudicating authority for personal insolvency (individuals and partnerships). A builder company's insolvency is adjudicated by NCLT.

Value Addition:
• The threshold for homebuyer joint filing: 100 allottees OR 10% of total allottees in a project, whichever is less — introduced to reduce frivolous individual filings.
• The 2018 amendment was challenged in Pioneer Urban Land vs. Union of India (2019) and upheld by the Supreme Court.
• Homebuyers rank as Financial Creditors in the CoC — they vote alongside banks on the resolution plan.

solution.concept_anchor: Pre-IBC fragmented framework — SICA, SARFAESI, RDDBFI — not FEMA
solution.strong_distractor: b — RDDBFI is a less commonly known acronym. Students who are unfamiliar with the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act may select it as the 'odd one out' because it sounds technical and unfamiliar, while SICA and SARFAESI are more frequently discussed.
elimination_logic: Identify the common category: laws that governed debt recovery, stressed asset resolution, or insolvency in the pre-IBC era.
SICA (Sick Industrial Companies Act, 1985) — pre-IBC mechanism for sick company rehabilitation; belongs here.
SARFAESI (Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002) — pre-IBC secured creditor enforcement; belongs here.
RDDBFI (Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993) — established DRTs for debt recovery; belongs here.

FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999) — governs cross-border foreign exchange transactions; it is NOT a debt recovery or insolvency statute and is not part of the pre-IBC stressed asset framework.
FEMA is the odd one out → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here presents four acronyms from financial law — three from the insolvency/debt recovery domain and one from foreign exchange regulation. FEMA sounds like it could be related to 'financial asset management' and is a financial sector law, making it superficially plausible. Students who cannot place RDDBFI precisely may eliminate it as unfamiliar rather than recognising FEMA's entirely different regulatory domain.
solution.final_explanation:
IBC 2016 was designed to replace a fragmented landscape of debt recovery and insolvency laws.

• Option (a) — SICA, 1985: Belongs here. The Sick Industrial Companies Act created the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) for rehabilitation of sick companies — a major pre-IBC mechanism that IBC replaced.
• Option (b) — RDDBFI Act, 1993: Belongs here. This Act established Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) to expedite recovery of bank dues — part of the pre-IBC debt recovery ecosystem that IBC works alongside.
• Option (c) — FEMA, 1999: Odd one out. The Foreign Exchange Management Act governs cross-border foreign exchange transactions and capital account controls — it has no role in domestic debt recovery or insolvency resolution.
• Option (d) — SARFAESI, 2002: Belongs here. SARFAESI empowers secured creditors to enforce security interests without court intervention — a key pre-IBC and coexisting mechanism for stressed asset resolution.

Value Addition:
• IBC repealed SICA and the Presidency Towns Insolvency Act but did NOT repeal SARFAESI or RDDBFI.
• The BLRC identified 12+ overlapping laws as the problem — IBC consolidated and clarified priority.
• BIFR under SICA was notorious for delays — cases lingered for decades, allowing promoters to delay resolution indefinitely.

solution.concept_anchor: Fresh Start Process — income, asset, and debt eligibility thresholds
solution.strong_distractor: c — The ₹1 lakh annual income figure sounds plausible as a poverty-level threshold for a debt relief process aimed at the most economically vulnerable individuals.
elimination_logic: Recall Fresh Start eligibility from Part III of IBC: aimed at the most economically distressed individuals.
The three thresholds under the Fresh Start Process: annual income ≤ ₹60,000; total assets ≤ ₹20,000; qualifying debt ≤ ₹35,000.
Eliminate (b): ₹1,20,000 income is double the actual ₹60,000 ceiling — too high.
Eliminate (c): ₹1,00,000 income sounds conservative but is still significantly above ₹60,000 — wrong.
Eliminate (d): ₹40,000 income is below the actual threshold — wrong in the opposite direction.
Confirm (a): Annual income ≤ ₹60,000, assets ≤ ₹20,000, and qualifying debt ≤ ₹35,000 match the statutory thresholds.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap here operates within the numerical range — students who have a general sense that the Fresh Start Process targets very poor individuals may estimate the income threshold anywhere between ₹40,000 and ₹1,20,000. The specific ₹60,000 annual income ceiling (₹5,000/month) is a precise figure that can only be recalled, not estimated. Distractors at ₹1 lakh and ₹1.2 lakh are the most attractive because they sound like 'reasonable' poverty thresholds.
solution.final_explanation:
The Fresh Start Process under Part III of IBC targets the most economically distressed individual debtors — those who have no realistic capacity to repay but have minimal assets that distinguish them from truly insolvent individuals.

• Option (a) — Correct: The statutory thresholds are annual income ≤ ₹60,000, total assets ≤ ₹20,000, and qualifying debt ≤ ₹35,000. Meeting these thresholds allows an individual to seek a fresh start by having qualifying debts discharged.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: ₹1,20,000 annual income (₹10,000/month) is double the statutory ceiling — too high to qualify.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: ₹1,00,000 annual income is above the ₹60,000 ceiling — incorrect threshold.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: ₹40,000 annual income is below the actual threshold — wrong in the downward direction.

Value Addition:
• The Fresh Start Process is adjudicated by DRT (not NCLT) — consistent with Part III's DRT-based architecture.
• Qualifying debt under Fresh Start must not include debt incurred by fraud.
• Part III of IBC has not been fully operationalised — the personal insolvency processes exist in statute but are not actively implemented, making awareness questions (rather than operational ones) the likely exam format.

solution.concept_anchor: Related party financial creditors excluded from CoC — Section 21(2)

statement_analysis.statement: A financial creditor who is a related party of the Corporate Debtor is excluded from the Committee of Creditors and cannot vote on any resolution plan.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 21(2) of IBC expressly excludes related party financial creditors from membership of the CoC — they cannot attend or vote. The rationale is conflict of interest: related parties may act to protect the promoter's interests rather than creditors' collective interest.

statement_analysis.statement: Operational Creditors who hold claims above 10% of the total debt may attend CoC meetings with voting rights proportional to their claims.
statement_analysis.reason: Operational Creditors above the 10% threshold may attend CoC meetings and make representations — but they have NO voting rights whatsoever. Voting in CoC is exclusively for Financial Creditors.

statement_analysis.statement: A decision by the Committee of Creditors to liquidate the Corporate Debtor requires a vote of not less than 66% of the total voting share of financial creditors.
statement_analysis.reason: The liquidation decision is a 'key decision' under IBC requiring a 66% supermajority vote of the CoC — the same threshold as for approving a resolution plan.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know Operational Creditors above a threshold have 'rights' in the CoC may incorrectly recall these as 'voting rights with proportional share,' making Statement 2 appear correct and leading to 'all three correct' as the answer.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 as correct — Section 21(2) explicitly excludes related party financial creditors from CoC. This is a clear statutory provision.
Identify Statement 2 as incorrect — Operational Creditors have NO voting rights regardless of their claim size; the 10% threshold grants only attendance and representation rights.
Confirm Statement 3 as correct — the 66% supermajority is required for both resolution plan approval and liquidation vote.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 adds 'voting rights' to what are actually representation-only rights for Operational Creditors above 10%. This is one of IBC's most carefully calibrated design choices — Operational Creditors participate in information sharing (they attend CoC meetings) but are excluded from commercial decision-making (no votes). Adding 'proportional voting' converts a partial right into a full right, creating a false statement that feels progressive and fair.
solution.final_explanation:
CoC composition and voting rules reflect IBC's deliberate creditor hierarchy.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 21(2) disqualifies related party financial creditors from the CoC. A subsidiary or sister concern of the corporate debtor cannot vote — this prevents the promoter from influencing the resolution plan through controlled entities.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Operational Creditors above 10% of total debt may attend CoC meetings and make representations — but they have absolutely NO voting rights. The 10% threshold is for attendance, not voting. This distinction was affirmed in Swiss Ribbons.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The liquidation decision requires 66% of total financial creditor voting share — the same threshold as resolution plan approval. Routine decisions (like issuing public announcement or extending CIRP timeline) require 51%.

Value Addition:
• The three 66% decisions: (i) approve resolution plan, (ii) decide to liquidate, (iii) replace the IRP/RP.
• Related party exclusion from CoC is a bright-line rule — no exceptions based on the size of the related party's claim.
• CoC has the power to appoint insolvency professionals for specific tasks (e.g., valuers) and to monitor the RP's performance.

solution.concept_anchor: CIRP vs. PPIRP vs. Fast Track CIRP — timelines and eligibility
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know PPIRP has a shorter timeline than CIRP may guess 90 days for PPIRP (confusing it with Fast Track CIRP's 90-day timeline) and then match incorrectly across the table.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Regular CIRP — the well-known 330-day outer limit; maps to A → 3.
PPIRP is for MSMEs with a 120-day timeline (faster than CIRP but longer than Fast Track); maps to B → 4.
Fast Track CIRP under Section 55 has a 90-day timeline (extendable by 45 days); maps to C → 1.
Voluntary Liquidation under Section 59 is not time-bound in the same way — it is for solvent companies winding up; maps to D → 2.
A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap places PPIRP's 120-day timeline at risk of being confused with Fast Track CIRP's 90-day timeline and vice versa. Both are 'fast' alternatives to the 330-day CIRP, and students who know both figures but cannot attach them precisely to the correct process will produce wrong matches. The key anchor: PPIRP (120 days) > Fast Track CIRP (90 days), and both are faster than regular CIRP (330 days).
solution.final_explanation:
IBC provides multiple resolution and winding-up tracks with distinct timelines tailored to different debtor profiles.

Correct matching:
• A (Regular CIRP) → 3 (330 days including litigation): The 2019 amendment set a mandatory 330-day outer limit, after which NCLT must order liquidation.
• B (PPIRP for MSMEs) → 4 (120 days): Introduced in 2021, PPIRP's debtor-in-possession design comes with a 120-day timeline — faster than CIRP but longer than Fast Track CIRP.
• C (Fast Track CIRP) → 1 (90 days, extendable by 45 days): Section 55's Fast Track applies to small companies, early-stage start-ups, and unlisted companies with minimal assets.
• D (Voluntary Liquidation) → 2 (Solvent company winding up — no fixed CIRP timeline): Voluntary Liquidation under Section 59 is not an insolvency proceeding — there is no creditor-driven timeline. The liquidator must complete distribution within a defined period but the process differs structurally.

A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 → option (b).

Value Addition:
• PPIRP's base resolution plan must be creditor-approved before NCLT admission — unique pre-admission feature.
• Fast Track CIRP has seen very low utilisation in practice — an awareness fact likely to be tested.
• Regular CIRP's 330-day limit was introduced specifically because courts were allowing indefinite extensions, defeating IBC's time-bound objective.

solution.concept_anchor: SARFAESI threshold vs. IBC CIRP threshold — different minimum amounts
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know IBC's ₹1 crore threshold and SARFAESI's lower threshold may incorrectly recall SARFAESI as ₹10 lakh (a round figure that sounds like a natural entry point for secured creditor action) rather than the actual ₹1 lakh.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): SARFAESI minimum is ₹1 lakh, not ₹10 lakh — this is the original SARFAESI threshold for secured asset enforcement.
Eliminate (b): IBC CIRP minimum is ₹1 crore (post-COVID amendment), not ₹10 lakh.
Eliminate (c): This reverses the thresholds entirely — SARFAESI is lower than IBC, not higher.
Confirm (d): SARFAESI applies to secured debts of ₹1 lakh or more; IBC CIRP applies to defaults of ₹1 crore or more — the IBC threshold is 100 times higher than SARFAESI's original threshold.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap confuses ₹1 lakh (SARFAESI) with ₹10 lakh or ₹1 crore (IBC-related thresholds). The ₹1 crore CIRP threshold is frequently memorised; ₹1 lakh for SARFAESI is less commonly recalled precisely. Additionally, ₹10 lakh appears in PPIRP's default window (₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore), creating further confusion among students who have memorised multiple thresholds without anchoring each to its source statute.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the different debt thresholds across IBC and SARFAESI is critical for comparative questions.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: SARFAESI's minimum threshold is ₹1 lakh (not ₹10 lakh) for a secured creditor to initiate enforcement action against a borrower's secured assets without court intervention.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The IBC CIRP minimum threshold is ₹1 crore (post-COVID amendment from ₹1 lakh). ₹10 lakh is the lower end of the PPIRP window for MSMEs — not the CIRP threshold.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: This option reverses the relationship — SARFAESI has the lower threshold (₹1 lakh) and IBC has the higher one (₹1 crore).
• Option (d) — Correct: SARFAESI applies to secured debts ≥ ₹1 lakh; IBC CIRP applies to defaults ≥ ₹1 crore for companies. This means a secured creditor with a ₹50 lakh defaulting loan can act under SARFAESI but NOT initiate CIRP.

Value Addition:
• Pre-COVID IBC threshold was ₹1 lakh — identical to SARFAESI's threshold. The COVID-19 ordinance (March 2020) raised CIRP threshold to ₹1 crore.
• PPIRP window: ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore default — sits between the two thresholds.
• SARFAESI is faster for a single secured creditor because it does not require NCLT admission — the bank can directly auction the asset.

solution.concept_anchor: Vidarbha Industries — NCLT discretion on Section 7 admission

statement_analysis.statement: In Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. vs. Axis Bank (2022), the Supreme Court held that the National Company Law Tribunal has discretionary power to admit or reject an application under Section 7 of IBC even when the applicant has conclusively proved the existence of a default.
statement_analysis.reason: The Vidarbha Industries judgment held that proof of default does not automatically compel NCLT to admit a Section 7 application — NCLT retains discretion to consider other factors (like ongoing regulatory proceedings that may provide relief), making admission non-automatic.

statement_analysis.statement: The Vidarbha Industries judgment was unanimously welcomed by the insolvency law community as it strengthened the creditor-friendly design of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.
statement_analysis.reason: The Vidarbha Industries judgment was widely criticised as controversial — it was seen as potentially undermining IBC's creditor-friendly, time-bound design by giving NCLT discretion to delay or refuse admission even when default is proved, potentially reintroducing BIFR-era delays.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Wait: correct_option IS (a). The strong distractor is (c), which would mark Statement 1 as incorrect (for students who believe admission under Section 7 is always automatic on proof of default).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Vidarbha Industries (2022) did hold that NCLT has discretion even after proof of default — this is the controversial but correct ratio of the judgment. Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: The judgment was NOT welcomed — it was highly controversial and criticised for potentially weakening IBC's creditor-in-control design. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 2 takes the factual core of Vidarbha Industries (a controversial judgment) and recharacterises it as 'welcomed by the insolvency community' — a 180-degree reversal of reality. A student who knows the judgment exists but has only surface-level awareness of its content may accept the mischaracterisation. The specific judgment knowledge required is not just 'what it held' but 'how it was received' — a nuanced layer that separates depth of preparation.
solution.final_explanation:
The Vidarbha Industries judgment (2022) is among the most debated IBC decisions in recent years.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Supreme Court in Vidarbha Industries held that when a Financial Creditor files under Section 7, proving default does not automatically oblige NCLT to admit the application. NCLT retains discretion — it can consider factors like ongoing regulatory proceedings that might resolve the debtor's situation without insolvency. This was a departure from the earlier understanding that admission was nearly automatic on proof of default.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The judgment was not welcomed — it triggered significant concern among creditors, insolvency practitioners, and academics. Critics argued it reintroduced judicial discretion in a code explicitly designed to reduce it, potentially allowing debtors to resist admission by pointing to other pending proceedings — reminiscent of the delays under SICA/BIFR.

Value Addition:
• The Vidarbha Industries judgment has been distinguished in subsequent cases — its full impact on Section 7 admissions remains an evolving area of IBC jurisprudence.
• Section 7's design intention was to make Financial Creditor applications quickly admitted — Vidarbha Industries complicated this by introducing a balancing exercise.
• The Swiss Ribbons case (2019) had earlier upheld IBC's design as constitutionally valid — Vidarbha Industries created a tension within IBC jurisprudence that courts are still resolving.

solution.concept_anchor: FSP insolvency — administrator (not RP), different regulatory involvement

statement_analysis.statement: The Financial Resolution and Deposit Insurance Bill, 2017 was enacted into law and currently provides the primary legislative framework for the resolution of banks and insurance companies in India.
statement_analysis.reason: The FRDI Bill 2017 was withdrawn by the government in 2018 amid public controversy over its 'bail-in' clause. It was never enacted. The framework for FSP insolvency currently rests on Section 227 of IBC and the IBC (Insolvency and Liquidation Proceedings of Financial Service Providers) Rules 2019.

statement_analysis.statement: When insolvency proceedings are initiated against a Financial Service Provider under the special rules notified under Section 227 of IBC, an Administrator (and not a Resolution Professional) is appointed to manage the entity.
statement_analysis.reason: The FSP Rules 2019 prescribe that an Administrator — not an RP — is appointed for FSP insolvency. The sectoral regulator (RBI, IRDAI, or SEBI) nominates or concurs in the appointment of this Administrator.

statement_analysis.statement: The resolution of Yes Bank in 2020 was conducted under the special IBC provisions for Financial Service Providers notified under Section 227.
statement_analysis.reason: Yes Bank's resolution in 2020 was handled through the RBI's powers under the Banking Regulation Act — specifically the Yes Bank Ltd. Reconstruction Scheme 2020, which involved a State Bank of India-led consortium taking a stake. It was NOT conducted under IBC's FSP provisions.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know that an Administrator is appointed in FSP insolvency (Statement 2 is correct) may doubt Statement 3's accuracy and assume Yes Bank was resolved under IBC FSP provisions — since the discussion of FSP resolution under IBC prominently featured Yes Bank as a test case.
elimination_logic: Identify Statement 1 as incorrect — the FRDI Bill was withdrawn in 2018, never enacted; its 'bail-in' clause caused depositor panic.
Confirm Statement 2 as correct — Administrator (not RP) is the correct official in FSP insolvency under Section 227 rules.
Identify Statement 3 as incorrect — Yes Bank was resolved through RBI's Banking Regulation Act powers and a reconstruction scheme, not through IBC FSP provisions.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct; since the stem asks which is NOT correct → option naming '1 and 3 only' = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the fact that Yes Bank is frequently cited as an example when discussing FSP resolution under IBC. The entity-swap occurs between the Banking Regulation Act (the actual mechanism) and IBC's Section 227 rules (the mechanism wrongly attributed). Students who have read about Yes Bank in the context of FSP resolution may conflate the conceptual discussion of IBC's FSP framework with its actual application in the Yes Bank case.
solution.final_explanation:
The resolution of Financial Service Providers in India has used multiple mechanisms — not all under IBC.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The FRDI Bill 2017 was introduced but withdrawn in August 2018 due to public outcry over the bail-in clause (which allowed failing banks to convert depositors' savings into equity to absorb losses). The current FSP insolvency framework is the IBC (Insolvency and Liquidation Proceedings of Financial Service Providers) Rules 2019 under Section 227.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Under the FSP Rules 2019, an Administrator is appointed (not a Resolution Professional as in CIRP). The relevant sectoral regulator nominates or concurs — RBI for banks/NBFCs, IRDAI for insurers, SEBI for market entities.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Yes Bank's resolution in March 2020 was executed under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — specifically the Yes Bank Ltd. Reconstruction Scheme 2020, which saw SBI and private banks acquiring a stake under RBI's direction. IBC's FSP provisions were not invoked.

Value Addition:
• IL&FS resolution (2018–2019) used the Companies Act route with NCLAT supervision — also not IBC's FSP provisions.
• DHFL insolvency (2021) was the first major NBFC resolution actually conducted under IBC's FSP Rules 2019.
• Bail-in vs. bail-out: Bail-in uses existing liabilities (including deposits) to recapitalise; bail-out uses public funds — the FRDI controversy centred on the bail-in clause.

solution.concept_anchor: IBBI enforcement powers — penalty ceiling, suo motu powers, quasi-judicial separation

statement_analysis.statement: IBBI can initiate inspection of an Insolvency Professional's conduct on its own motion, without waiting for a formal complaint from an aggrieved party.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 218 of IBC empowers IBBI to inspect IPs, IPAs, and IUs suo motu — the regulator does not require a complaint to initiate inspection. This proactive power is fundamental to IBBI's oversight role.

statement_analysis.statement: The maximum monetary penalty IBBI can impose on an Insolvency Professional is ₹5 crore, or three times the amount of illegal gains, whichever is higher.
statement_analysis.reason: The maximum monetary penalty under IBC is ₹1 crore (not ₹5 crore), or three times the amount of profits made through the contravention, whichever is higher.

statement_analysis.statement: IBBI exercises quasi-judicial functions through an Adjudicating Officer mechanism that is kept separate from the investigation function — the same officer cannot investigate and adjudicate the same matter.
statement_analysis.reason: The separation of investigation and adjudication within IBBI is a due process safeguard — the investigating authority and the Adjudicating Officer are different, ensuring the adjudicator has not been influenced by the investigation.

statement_analysis.statement: IBBI is empowered to function as an appellate authority over NCLT orders in insolvency matters that involve registered Insolvency Professionals.
statement_analysis.reason: IBBI has no appellate authority over NCLT orders — it is purely a regulatory body. NCLT's appellate hierarchy runs to NCLAT and then the Supreme Court. IBBI's quasi-judicial function extends only to disciplinary proceedings against IPs, IPAs, and IUs.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know IBBI has both regulatory and quasi-judicial functions may incorrectly infer that this extends to appellate jurisdiction over NCLT, particularly in cases involving IP misconduct. Marking Statement 4 as correct would shift the count to three, selecting option (c).
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 as correct — suo motu inspection power is expressly provided under Section 218.
Identify Statement 2 as incorrect — the ceiling is ₹1 crore (not ₹5 crore); ₹5 crore is a fabricated figure designed to sound like an enhanced regulatory penalty.
Confirm Statement 3 as correct — separation of investigation and adjudication is a structural due process guarantee within IBBI.
Identify Statement 4 as incorrect — IBBI is a regulator, not an appellate authority; NCLT orders are appealed to NCLAT.
Two statements correct (1 and 3) → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's plausible fabrication uses ₹5 crore — a figure large enough to sound credible for a financial sector regulator (SEBI's penalties, for example, can run into crores). The actual ₹1 crore ceiling is lower than students might expect for a capital market context, making the fabricated ₹5 crore attractive. Statement 4's fabrication exploits the genuine confusion about IBBI's 'dual role' — students who know IBBI has both regulatory and quasi-judicial powers may not draw the precise line where that quasi-judicial power ends (at IP discipline, not NCLT appeals).
solution.final_explanation:
IBBI's enforcement powers are specific and bounded — understanding their precise scope is essential.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 1. Suo motu inspection power | Correct |
| 2. Maximum penalty ₹5 crore | Incorrect |
| 3. Separation of investigation and adjudication | Correct |
| 4. Appellate authority over NCLT | Incorrect |

Two statements are correct (1 and 3) → option (b).

Statement 2: The actual ceiling is ₹1 crore OR three times illegal gains — whichever is higher. ₹5 crore does not appear in IBC's penalty provisions.
Statement 4: IBBI's quasi-judicial function covers disciplinary proceedings against IPs, IPAs, and IUs only. It has zero appellate jurisdiction over NCLT orders.

Value Addition:
• IBBI can impose penalties cumulatively — each violation can attract a separate penalty up to the ceiling.
• The three-stage process (inspection → investigation → adjudication) mirrors the structure of other financial regulators like SEBI.
• IBBI's annual report to Parliament (through MCA) is the primary transparency mechanism — it is not subject to parliamentary questions in the way a ministry is.

solution.concept_anchor: IBC regulated entities — IPs, IPAs, IUs, their functions and examples
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know NeSL is an IU and ICSI is connected to insolvency may correctly match those two but then confuse IPA and IP roles — placing 'enroll and regulate IPs' with the individual professional category rather than the agency category.
elimination_logic: Anchor on NeSL — National e-Governance Services Ltd. is the only operational Information Utility; maps to C → 2 (stores authenticated financial data of debtors).
Anchor on ICSI-IIP — this is the IPA promoted by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India; maps to B → 4 (enroll and regulate individual IPs as an SRO).
Anchor on Insolvency Professional — an individual professional who manages CIRP/liquidation; maps to A → 3 (appointed as IRP on NCLT admission, manages debtor as going concern).
Anchor on Insolvency Professional Entity (IPE) — a firm (partnership/company) through which IPs operate; maps to D → 1 (entity through which IPs render services).
A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1 → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the functions of IPAs (enrollment of IPs) with individual IPs themselves. Students who know that IPAs are 'connected to IPs' may place the enrollment/regulation function with the IP category rather than the IPA category. The further subtlety is the IPE — a less commonly known entity — which sits between the IPA (institutional SRO) and the IP (individual professional), and which students may confuse with either.
solution.final_explanation:
The four regulated entity categories under IBBI have distinct functions that must be precisely matched.

• A (Insolvency Professional) → 3: An IP is an individual professional who takes charge during CIRP — appointed as IRP by NCLT initially, then managing the corporate debtor as a going concern, inviting resolution plans, and liaising with the CoC.
• B (Insolvency Professional Agency — ICSI-IIP) → 4: IPAs are SROs that enroll individual IPs, maintain professional standards, and exercise first-level discipline. ICSI-IIP, IIIPI, and ICAI-IIP are the three recognised IPAs.
• C (Information Utility — NeSL) → 2: NeSL stores authenticated financial information submitted by creditors, enabling rapid claims verification during CIRP. It is the only currently operational IU.
• D (Insolvency Professional Entity) → 1: An IPE is a firm (partnership or company) through which IPs provide services — it cannot itself act as IRP/RP but is the business vehicle of IPs.

A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1 → option (d).

Value Addition:
• IBBI regulates all four: IPs, IPAs, IUs, and IPEs — directly or through the IPA-IP chain.
• The two-tier architecture: IBBI → IPAs → IPs ensures sector self-regulation with apex oversight.
• IPEs were added as a regulated category to bring accountability to the firms through which IPs operate, closing a regulatory gap.

solution.concept_anchor: Liquidation — going concern sale option for liquidator
solution.strong_distractor: a — The word 'liquidation' is colloquially understood as breaking up and selling assets piecemeal. Students who associate liquidation exclusively with asset-by-asset sale will select (a), not knowing that IBC's liquidator has the power to sell the business as a going concern.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): A liquidator under IBC is NOT restricted to selling assets piecemeal. IBC expressly allows the liquidator to sell the business as a going concern — preserving employment and maximising value.

Eliminate (b): Liquidation can be triggered when no resolution plan is submitted OR approved within the timeline; when CoC decides (66%); or when the approved plan contravenes applicable law — not only when CoC unanimously agrees.
Eliminate (d): The liquidator does not require CoC approval to sell as a going concern — the CoC's role ends largely when liquidation is ordered; the liquidator has independent authority.
Confirm (c): Section 53's waterfall places CIRP/liquidation costs first — these costs include the liquidator's fees. Creditors receive proceeds only after costs are paid. This is correctly stated.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (a) limits the liquidator's powers to piecemeal asset sale — a restriction that does not exist in IBC. IBC's design deliberately includes going concern sale during liquidation as a value-maximisation tool. Students who equate 'liquidation' with 'breaking up the company' will select (a). The correct option (c) tests the waterfall's first priority — CIRP and liquidation costs — which is a precise, often overlooked fact.
solution.final_explanation:
IBC's liquidation process contains several features that deviate from traditional winding-up understanding.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The liquidator has the power to sell the business or a part of it as a going concern — this is an express option under Schedule I of the Liquidation Process Regulations. Piecemeal asset sale is just one of several modes of realisation.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Liquidation is triggered in three situations: (i) no resolution plan submitted or approved within the 330-day limit, (ii) CoC votes for liquidation by 66% (not unanimously), or (iii) the approved plan contravenes applicable law.
• Option (c) — Correct: The liquidation waterfall under Section 53 places CIRP costs and liquidation costs — including the liquidator's remuneration — as the first charge on liquidation proceeds. Creditors, including secured ones, receive distributions only after these costs are fully paid.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The liquidator acts independently once appointed — the CoC is dissolved or ceases to be active post-liquidation order. The liquidator does not need CoC approval for going concern sale.

Value Addition:
• Going concern sale in liquidation preserves employment and avoids destruction of business value — a key policy objective.
• A liquidator can be an IP registered with IBBI — the same pool as resolution professionals.
• If no resolution plan is feasible and no buyer emerges even in liquidation, the assets are distributed to creditors according to the Section 53 waterfall.

solution.concept_anchor: India's non-adoption of UNCITRAL Model Law — bilateral vs. multilateral approach
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both A (India has not adopted UNCITRAL Model Law) and R (Sections 234-235 exist as bilateral provisions) are true, and who see a surface causal link ('bilateral first, then multilateral') may select (a).
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. As of the knowledge cutoff, India has not adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency 1997, despite the 2018 Insolvency Law Committee recommendation.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Sections 234 and 235 of IBC provide the bilateral agreement mechanism as the existing (though underoperationalised) cross-border insolvency framework.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. India's non-adoption of the UNCITRAL Model Law is not because Sections 234 and 235 exist as bilateral alternatives — the non-adoption stems from legislative inertia, concerns about modified universalism's implications for Indian courts, and the complexity of adapting COMI to India's debtor profile. The existence of bilateral provisions in Sections 234-235 is a parallel feature, not the cause of UNCITRAL non-adoption.
Both A and R correct, R does not explain A → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap presents Sections 234-235 (bilateral mechanism) as the reason India has not adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law — implying 'we have bilateral provisions, so we don't need the multilateral framework.' This is a plausible but incorrect causal chain. The actual reasons for non-adoption are legislative complexity and concerns about jurisdiction — not the existence of bilateral provisions. Options (a) and (b) are the two candidate answers; the distinction rests entirely on whether R causes A.
solution.final_explanation:
India's cross-border insolvency architecture is characterised by framework provisions that exist but have not been activated.

Assertion (A): Correct. India has not adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency 1997. The Insolvency Law Committee (2018) recommended adoption with India-specific modifications, but this recommendation has not been legislatively implemented. Cross-border insolvency remains an incomplete area of IBC.

Reason (R): Correct as a factual statement. Sections 234 and 235 of IBC provide for bilateral agreements — Section 234 for treaties with foreign governments, Section 235 for assistance from foreign courts. However, no bilateral treaties have been operationalised.

Causal relationship: R does not correctly explain A. India's non-adoption of the UNCITRAL Model Law is a legislative and policy choice driven by concerns about modified universalism, the complexity of determining COMI for Indian debtors, and implementation challenges — not because bilateral provisions in Sections 234-235 exist as an alternative. The two are independent phenomena.

Correct option: (b)

Value Addition:
• COMI (Centre of Main Interests) determines which country's proceedings are 'main' under the UNCITRAL framework — typically where the debtor's head office is.
• Modified universalism under UNCITRAL: recognises foreign proceedings and coordinates between jurisdictions without full universalism.
• Countries that have adopted UNCITRAL Model Law include the USA, UK, Australia, Singapore — India's absence from this list is a noted gap in its insolvency framework.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

Reason (R): The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code already contains Sections 234 and 235 which provide for bilateral agreements with foreign governments and assistance from foreign courts as a mechanism for addressing cross-border insolvency situations.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct

solution.concept_anchor: IRP appointment authority — NCLT appoints IRP on admission
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know IBBI regulates insolvency professionals may incorrectly believe IBBI also appoints them in a specific case — confusing the regulator's enrollment function with the tribunal's appointment function.
elimination_logic: Recall that CIRP commences upon NCLT's admission of the insolvency application.
The IRP is appointed by NCLT at the time of admission — the applicant may propose a name, but the appointment order comes from NCLT.
IBBI regulates IPs in general but does not appoint the IRP in a specific case — that is NCLT's function.
The CoC can later replace the IRP with an RP by a 66% vote — but this is replacement, not initial appointment.
The blank must be filled with NCLT → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap places IBBI in the role of appointing the IRP — a plausible error because IBBI registers and regulates insolvency professionals. The critical distinction is between registration/regulation (IBBI's function) and appointment in a specific CIRP (NCLT's function). A student who knows IPs are 'under IBBI' but has not traced the appointment mechanism through the statute will substitute IBBI for NCLT.
solution.final_explanation:
The institutional choreography at CIRP commencement is precise and examinable.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs does not appoint IRPs in individual cases — MCA sets policy and oversees IBBI, but has no case-specific appointment role.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: IBBI registers and regulates insolvency professionals as a class but does not issue case-specific appointment orders for IRP roles.
• Option (c) — Correct: Upon admitting an insolvency application, the National Company Law Tribunal issues an order appointing the Interim Resolution Professional. The applicant (Financial or Operational Creditor) may propose a name, which NCLT typically accepts if the proposed IP is registered and has no conflict.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Committee of Creditors is constituted only after the IRP has been appointed and has collated creditor claims — the CoC cannot appoint the IRP because it does not exist before the IRP starts functioning.

Value Addition:
• The IRP serves until the CoC is constituted and chooses to replace the IRP with an RP (66% vote required).
• An IP proposed as IRP must have no conflict of interest with the corporate debtor or its creditors.
• IBBI maintains a panel of registered IPs from which applicants can select — but the formal appointment is NCLT's prerogative.
